cues.text: Let us now turn to some additional SDN use cases, and then look at what happens when things go wrong.
Start with the data centre.
In a data centre, software-defined networking, or SDN, can do four things.
First, it can provision tenant overlays.
A tenant is a customer or a group of users sharing the same physical infrastructure, and an overlay is a virtual network built on top of the physical one, so each tenant gets its own logical network.
Second, SDN can isolate workloads, keeping one workload separated from another.
Third, it can dynamically select paths, choosing routes through the network as conditions change.
And fourth, it can expose policy APIs to cloud orchestrators.
An API, or application programming interface, is a defined way for software to make requests of other software.
So the cloud orchestrator, which is the system that coordinates cloud resources, can use those policy APIs to request network behaviour automatically.
Now move to a wide area network, or WAN.
Here, central policy can choose links according to bandwidth, delay, cost or service constraints.

So instead of configuring each router separately, one central policy can say, for example, which link suits which kind of traffic, based on those four factors: bandwidth, delay, cost, and service constraints.
Then the campus.
In a campus network, a controller can automate authenticated access and exam-portal traffic policies.
In other words, the controller can help make sure that users are authenticated when they connect, and that traffic to and from the exam portal is handled according to defined policy.
The source then gives one important condition that applies to every one of these cases.
Each case requires compatible devices, topology information, controller resilience, monitoring and staged rollout.
Let me take those five requirements in turn.
Compatible devices: the switches and routers must actually support the control mechanism in use.
Topology information: the controller must know how the network is connected.
Controller resilience: the controller itself must be able to withstand failure.
Monitoring: you must observe what the network is really doing.
And staged rollout: changes are introduced in steps, not all at once.
That brings us to fault analysis.
Suppose a controller is unavailable.
What happens?
The source says that existing permanent flows may keep forwarding.
A flow here is a forwarding rule installed in a switch, and a permanent one does not expire.
Those may continue to work.
However, new flows requiring reactive decisions may fail.
Reactive means the switch has to ask the controller what to do when a new kind of traffic arrives, and if the controller cannot answer, that traffic may fail.
Also, expiring flows may disappear.
Flows with a timeout will eventually be removed, and without the controller they may not be replaced.
The source adds a qualification that we must keep: actual behaviour depends on switch fail-mode and configured rules.
Fail-mode is the setting that determines how a switch behaves when it loses contact with its controller.
So you cannot assume one outcome; it depends on that setting and on the rules that are configured.
Because of this, the source says to test controller failover, management-channel loss, inconsistent policy and rollback in an isolated lab.

Four things to test: controller failover, which is switching to a backup controller; management-channel loss, which is losing the connection between the switch and the controller; inconsistent policy, where rules disagree with one another; and rollback, which is returning to a previous working configuration.
All of this should be done in an isolated lab, not on the live network.
And here is the key lesson of this passage: redundancy is a design property that must be measured, not inferred from the word centralised.
Just because a controller is described as centralised does not tell you whether the system is redundant.
You must test and measure it.
Finally, an intent example.
Intent means describing the outcome you want, rather than the individual device settings.
The example has three requirements: require staff access to an HR service, deny student access, and preserve a minimum voice queue.
The voice queue requirement means voice traffic keeps a guaranteed minimum share of capacity.
The source then gives the process.
First, translate desired outcomes to scoped rules.
Second, validate overlaps and priorities, because two rules may match the same traffic, and the priority decides which one wins.
Third, deploy.
Fourth, inspect flow counters, which show how many packets have matched each rule.
Fifth, perform positive and negative tests: a positive test confirms that staff can reach the HR service, and a negative test confirms that students cannot.
Then, reconcile actual state with intent, meaning compare what the network is really doing with what you wanted, and correct any difference.
Last, two security principles.
Separate management authority from application traffic, so that the channel used to control the network is not mixed up with ordinary user traffic.
And limit controller permissions, so the controller has only the access it needs.
